say: Welcome back, inquirers! Today’s problems all have a story with a BEFORE and an AFTER: someone spends money, gives away stickers, or gets a bit older.
The trick that makes them easy is to notice what stays the same. Notice it, test it, explain why.

A jar has 120 marbles. I will turn over two cards. After each card, draw what is LEFT as a new bar and write how many marbles are left. Each card tells you what to take the fraction of: “of the jar” or “of what is left”. I will read it twice.
Volunteers: how did you find 1/3 of what was left? Show your bar if you like.
Ali has 18 counters and Mei has 6. Ali gives Mei counters one at a time. Before you move any, predict: what will happen to the total? To the difference?
Now both children get 2 more counters each time. Predict again: total or difference, which one stays the same?
Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks, and before you touch the objects. Silent thinking. I will show the clock. Then talk with your partner.
stuck: Stuck: make a table with four columns, Ali, Mei, total, difference, and fill one row after every move.
Not sure about the difference: line the two rows of counters up side by side and count the extra ones.
If a pair wants more: how many counters must Ali give so that Mei has 1/3 as many as Ali? (He gives 0: she already does, 6 is 1/3 of 18.) What about 3/5 as many? (Ali gives 3: 15 and 9.)

say: “Mei spent 2/5 on a bag, so I draw 5 parts and shade 2. Then 1/2 of the REMAINDER on shoes. The remainder is 3 parts and I can’t halve 3 parts nicely, so I cut every part into 2. Now there are 10 equal units: bag 4, shoes 3, left 3.”
“3 units are $27, so 1 unit is $9 and 10 units are $90. Check: bag $36, shoes $27, left $27. That adds to $90.”

“Ali gives Ben 14 cards. Did the total change? No, the cards only moved. So the total after is still 96. After, Ali has 1/3 as many as Ben: Ali 1 unit, Ben 3 units. 4 units = 96, 1 unit = 24. Ali had 14 more before: 38.”

do: Ask: “What stays the same in this story: the total, the difference, or one amount? How do you know?”
Ask: “Are your units all the same size? Point to one unit and tell me what it is worth.”
Ask: “Check your answer in the story. Does every sentence still work?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Draw the AFTER model first. That is the part with the fraction.”
Hint 2: “Which amount did not change? Label it with its number in BOTH models.”
Hint 3: “Find what 1 unit is worth, then work backwards to the start.”

do: Ask: “What stays the same in this story: the total, the difference, or one amount? How do you know?”
Ask: “Are your units all the same size? Point to one unit and tell me what it is worth.”
Ask: “Check your answer in the story. Does every sentence still work?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Draw the AFTER model first. That is the part with the fraction.”
Hint 2: “Which amount did not change? Label it with its number in BOTH models.”
Hint 3: “Find what 1 unit is worth, then work backwards to the start.”

say: “Ali has 50 marbles and Mei has 30. Ali gives Mei some marbles. Can the difference still be 20 afterwards?”
“When does the total stay the same, and when does the difference stay the same?”
ask: “Ali has 50 marbles and Mei has 30. Ali gives Mei some marbles. Can the difference still be 20 afterwards?”

Yes. If Ali gives Mei 20 marbles, Ali has 30 and Mei has 50: the difference is 20 again, but now Mei has more. The total is 80 the whole time. Giving between two people keeps the total the same; both getting (or spending) the same amount keeps the difference the same.

say: “Today you drew models with a before and an after, and you found the part that stays the same. Next time a story changes, ask yourself: what did NOT change?”
“Show me your exit ticket and collect your stamp.”

p5l3-title.note: Minutes 0 to 2 (opening, inside the 90-minute clock). Objective: Solve fraction word problems with units and before-and-after models: fraction of a remainder, giving between two people (the total stays the same), both getting or spending the same amount (the difference stays the same), and one amount that does not change. Thinking strategies today: DRAW A MODEL and ASK "WHAT STAYS THE SAME?" Materials: Mini whiteboard and marker, 24 counters or paper squares (two colours), paper strips for bar models, workbook, pencil. Online: The tutor shares the slides and builds each bar model click by click. Children draw their models on whiteboards and say what each model shows together on three. For the explore, children move 18 + 6 paper squares on the desk with the camera up as usual and check the table against the slide; or use the interactive version on the slide. Time plan (the exact minutes of this lesson; every lesson adds up to 90): opening 0 to 2, sneak-peek puzzles 2 to 6.5 (one check for both puzzles, no volunteer round, nobody is marked), warm-up 6.5 to 13 (one game round, four quick questions), explore 13 to 26.5 (pair work 6 minutes at most, then two questions together; a Go further what-if is on the explore slide for any pair that finishes), teaching 26.5 to 38.5 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 38.5 to 42.5, workbook page 1 42.5 to 56.5 (the questions without a star; after question 2 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder), check together 56.5 to 60, short teaching before page 2 60 to 61.5, workbook page 2 61.5 to 69.5 (alone: start with the questions named at the top, then choose; starred parts are take-home; nobody has to finish), check together 69.5 to 71.5, talk time 71.5 to 77 (you may say pass; volunteers first; the first step of the Investigation is take-home), exit ticket 77 to 83, reflection 83 to 85.5 (pass is always OK), stamp typed in the chat and goodbye 85.5 to 86.5, and the buffer 86.5 to 90 (floating time: spend it first if you run late, never fill it on purpose). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are open to every child and have no clock time. The tutor never announces who is on which page, and never splits a pair unless both children agree. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." SPINE: Today's tool is Work backwards. Reverse the operations from the result, then confirm by running forwards. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook.

p5l3-check.note: Minutes 2 to 6.5. SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES. Show puzzle 1 and give about a minute; click to show the short answer later. Then show puzzle 2 and give about a minute. Open with one line only: "Guessing is welcome. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is an access puzzle: any child can try it with objects, drawing or counting, so everyone can start well. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. ONE check for both puzzles: after puzzle 2, everyone says the answers together on three (face to face, you may glance at papers held low as you walk round; online, nothing is held up to the camera). Then click through the two short answers and say each with one short reason. NO volunteer round here (volunteers come in the talk time). Never boards in front of the group, never read out answers with names, no tally, no ranking. Never record scores. Answers and what to listen for. Q1: (a) 36. (b) 24 years older now, and 24 years older when Ben is 12: the gap does not change.; Q2: 10. The TOTAL stays 60, so each has 30 afterwards and Ali gives 40 − 30 = 10. Counters or a drawing help. SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES (about 4.5 minutes). Show the two puzzles one at a time. Say one line only: "Guessing is welcome. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is one that any child can try with objects, drawing or counting, so everybody can start well. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. Answers are shown PRIVATELY, never on boards in front of the group. Face to face: children write on their own paper and show it only to you as you walk round. Online: children say the answers together on three; nothing is held up to the camera. Do not read answers out with names, do not keep a tally, do not rank. Use ONE check for both puzzles (after puzzle 2, everyone says the answers together on three), then click through the answers and say each one with one short reason. There is NO volunteer round in the sneak-peek; volunteers come in the talk time. Never choose a child because you saw a wrong answer. Never record scores. Choosing a start: every child has the same neutral line on workbook page 1: "After question 2 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." (The number is the last question on page 1 of this lesson.) Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Never single out a child by name and never announce who is on which page. Pairs are not split unless BOTH children agree. Any child may swap at any time.

p5l3-warm1.note: Minutes 6.5 to 9.5. What is left? Children have mini whiteboards. Say "Card 1" and read it; give thinking time; children write the number left and say the answer together on three; click to show the answer. Then Card 2. Talk: Card 2 says "of what is left", so we take 1/3 of 90, not 1/3 of 120 (90 − 30 = 60). Tutor extension if the group is ready: a third card, give away 5/6 of what is left (5/6 of 60 is 50, so 10 are left). Ask: "Did anyone take 1/3 of 120? What would that give? (40; the story would be different.)" The bar shows the first card: 120 is cut into 12 units of 10, and 1/4 is 3 units. Listen for children who draw the remainder as a new bar. Answers: 90, 60. This is the idea of the whole lesson: after each step the amount we start from changes.

p5l3-warm2.note: Minutes 9.5 to 13. Whiteboards: read each question aloud, give thinking time, write on boards, say the answer together on three, click to show. Answers: 1) 18 (45 ÷ 5 = 9, 9 × 2). 2) 36 (3 units = 27, 1 unit = 9, 4 units = 36). 3) 1/4 (1/3 of 3 quarters is 1 quarter). 4) Still 12: both get the same, so the gap does not change. Question 4 is one of the two big ideas of today (the other is that the total stays the same when cards move between two children); do not explain yet, just ask "why?" and collect ideas. If you are short of time, skip question 4.

p5l3-explore1.note: Minutes 13 to 26.5 (the whole explore; this slide 13 to 22.5). Pairs use 24 counters or paper squares (online: paper squares on the desk, camera up as usual; check the table against the slide). Predict first: when Ali gives counters away, does the total change? Does the difference change? Let pairs record in two tables: Ali, Mei, total, difference. Second table: start again at 18 and 6 and give BOTH children 2 more each time. Anyone who wants more (open to every pair): find when Mei has 1/3 as many as Ali (right at the start: 18 and 6), and 3/5 as many (after Ali gives 3: 15 and 9). PROTECTED THINK TIME: before the pairs touch anything, say "Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks" and show the clock; then pairs talk and start. PAIR WORK IS CAPPED AT 6 MINUTES: say "Pencils down" at minute 22.5 and bring the group back (the minutes before that include the 30 seconds of thinking, finding materials and, in lessons that use them, the move to and from breakout rooms). GO FURTHER (say it as soon as a pair has finished the task): any pair that finishes early may try the what-if question on the next slide. It is open to every pair, not a reward. Answer: No for 25: equal shares would be 12 and a half each, so an odd total can never be shared equally. With 24 (18 and 6) it works: 12 each after Ali gives 6. The total never changes when they only swap counters.

p5l3-explore2.note: Minutes 22.5 to 26.5. Pencils down: gather the pairs. Build one table on the board and ask for each row. Answers: 1) The total: 24 every time Ali gives Mei counters (16 and 8, 15 and 9 …). 2) The difference: 12 every time both get 2 more (20 and 8, 22 and 10 …). (Not asked together: when did Mei have 1/2 as many as Ali? After Ali gives 2 (16 and 8), and after both get 6 more (24 and 12).) Ask: "Why does the total stay the same when Ali gives and the difference stay the same when both get?" Do NOT tell: the next slides name these two ideas. TWO questions together only (about a minute each), then move on. GO FURTHER what-if (open to every pair as soon as it has finished; nobody waits): No for 25: equal shares would be 12 and a half each, so an odd total can never be shared equally. With 24 (18 and 6) it works: 12 each after Ali gives 6. The total never changes when they only swap counters.

p5l3-teach1.note: Minutes 26.5 to 29. Teach. Read the problem twice. Ask: "Is the 1/2 half of her money or half of what is left?" Click order: step 1, the cut bar, steps 2 and 3. Think-aloud: "2/5 on the bag means I draw 5 parts and shade 2. That leaves 3 parts. Half of the REMAINDER is half of 3 parts, and I cannot halve 3 parts neatly, so I cut every part into 2 pieces. Now every unit is the same size. The bag is 4 units, the remainder is 6 units, shoes are 3 units, and 3 units are left." Then: "3 units are $27 so one unit is $9; the whole bar is 10 units, $90." Check by going forwards: bag 2/5 of 90 = 36; remainder 54; shoes 27; left 27. Common error: taking 1/2 of the WHOLE for the shoes.

p5l3-try1.note: Minutes 29 to 31.5. Whiteboards. a) Game 1/2 (4 of 8 units); remainder 4 units; lunch 1/4 of 4 units = 1 unit; left 3 units = $18, 1 unit = $6, 8 units = $48. Check: game $24, remainder $24, lunch $6, left $18. b) 10 units: Saturday 3; remainder 7; Sunday 2/7 of 7 = 2; left 5 units = 25 pages; 1 unit = 5; book 50 pages. Check: 15 read, 35 left, 10 read Sunday, 25 left. (Two items only.)

p5l3-teach2.note: Minutes 31.5 to 34. Teach. Ask first: "Did the total change when Ali gave Ben some cards?" Draw the AFTER model first: it is the part with the fraction. Click order: step 1, step 2, then the bars fill in with the numbers, then step 3. Think-aloud: "Ali has 1/3 as many as Ben, so Ali is 1 unit and Ben is 3 units. The total is 4 units and that is 96, so a unit is 24. Ali has 24 AFTER giving away 14. To go back to BEFORE I add the 14 back: 38." Stress going backwards from after to before. Check: before 38 + 58 = 96.

p5l3-try2.note: Minutes 34 to 36.5. Whiteboards. a) The total is 60, so 30 each; Ali gives 45 − 30 = 15 (check: 30 and 30). b) After: Ben 1 unit, Ali 2 units, 3 units = 72, 1 unit = 24, so Ben has 24 after and had 24 + 6 = 30 at first. (Two items only.)

p5l3-key.note: Minutes 36.5 to 38.5. Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Taking the second fraction of the whole amount instead of the remainder (1/4 of the remainder read as 1/4 of all the money). (2) Thinking the difference goes down by 10 when one person gives the other 10 (it goes down by 20: one loses 10, the other gains 10). (3) Keeping the units from the Before model when the thing that stays the same is a different amount, so the units in the two models are not the same size.

p5l3-break.note: Minutes 38.5 to 42.5. 4 minutes. Online: children stand in view of the camera. Ask for 1/2 of the whole with arms (one arm up), 1/4, then 3/4. Ask: "What is 1/2 of 1/2?" and have them show it with their arms (1/4). Then a drink of water.

p5l3-ws1.note: Minutes 42.5 to 56.5. Walk around. Ask "What stays the same in this story?" before giving any help. Q1 uses the remainder idea from the worked example, Q2 the "total stays the same" idea. Page 1 has only Q1 and Q2 (Q3, the marbles, is on page 2 and is take-home). Everyone sees the same neutral line: "After question 2 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." (Question 2 is the last question to do in class on page 1 of this lesson.) Never announce who is on which page and never name a child in front of the group. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: "when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Do not split a pair unless BOTH children agree. Think harder is the next pages after the Investigation page in the workbook. IN CLASS NOW: Q1 (a) (b) (c) and Q2 (a) (b). Parts marked with a star in the workbook are take-home: say so once ("the starred parts are for home") and do not wait for them.

p5l3-ws1ans.note: Minutes 56.5 to 60. Click each answer after a pair explains theirs. Q1: pen = 1/4 of 2/3 = 1/6; 6 units, 3 units left = $36, 1 unit = $12; total $72; book 2 units = $24, pen 1 unit = $12. Q2b: after, Siti 3 units and Mei 4 units = 84, 1 unit = 12; Siti 36 after, so 36 + 12 = 48 at first; Mei 84 − 48 = 36. Q3a: Ali has 20 more; if he gives 10, Ali 40 and Ben 40; if he gave 20, Ali 30 and Ben 50, the gap flips. Q3b: total 80, 8 units, 1 unit = 10, Ali 30 and Ben 50 after giving 20.

p5l3-teachdiff.note: Minutes 60 to 61.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4: both get the same amount of money). Ask first: "Everyone gets one year older every year. Does the gap between Mei and her mother change?" No. Click: step 1, then the later model, then steps 2 and 3. Think-aloud: "The gap is 28 now and it will be 28 later. Later, Mei is 1 unit and Mum is 3 units, so the gap is 2 units. 2 units are 28, so 1 unit is 14. Mei is 14 later; she is 8 now; 6 years." Link to the worksheet: "Giving each person the same money is just like each person getting one year older: the difference stays the same." Do the same story with money: both get $5 more, the gap is unchanged.

p5l3-ws2.note: Minutes 61.5 to 69.5. Children work alone on Q4 only; Q3 and Q5 are take-home (starred). Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson, especially children who keep the total the same when the stay-the-same amount is the difference. Page 2 is a menu, not a wall. Everyone sees the same line: start with Q4 (a) (b), then choose. Nobody has to finish; stop at minute 69.5 whatever has been done, because the check-together slide gives every answer with its explanation. Starred parts are take-home (their answers are on the check slide for you; do not spend class time on them). Walk round, ask "what could you try first?", and give the first hint before any answer.

p5l3-ws2ans.note: Minutes 69.5 to 71.5. One child explains Q4; click through the rest (Q3 and Q5 are take-home, their answers are here for you). Click each answer after a child explains. Q4: the difference $50 − $26 = $24 stays $24; after, Ali 2 units and Ravi 3 units, so 1 unit = $24, Ali has $48 after, so the mother gave $48 − $26 = $22 (check: $72 and $48; 48 is 2/3 of 72). Q5: 12 red and 8 blue, 20 beads. 10 red are added, so the jar has 30 beads. Blue is 8 of 20 = 2/5 at first and 8 of 30 = 4/15 now. Only red was added, so blue is the part that does not change; the blue fraction gets smaller because the whole gets bigger. The full problem (3/7 red, then 30 red added, 3/5 red) is Think harder A2: blue 4 units at first and 2 parts of 5 after, so the whole box is 10 units; red 3 units then 6 units, so 30 = 3 units, 1 unit = 10, 70 beads at first and 100 now.

p5l3-stretch.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Think harder questions A1 to A4 (the same as the workbook). Answers: A1) $120 (20 units: Monday 5 units, Tuesday 6 units; 11 units = $66, so 1 unit = $6) A2) 70 at first, 100 now (the blue beads did not change: 4 units at first, and 2 parts of 5 after, so 1 part = 2 units and the whole box is 10 units; red 3 units at first and 6 units now, so 3 units = 30 and 1 unit = 10) A3) 1 year ago (the difference, 32, is 4 units; 1 unit = 8: son 8, Mrs Tan 40) A4) $80 (Ben 2 units, Siti 1 unit + $20; 3 units = $120, 1 unit = $40)

p5l3-stretch2.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Think harder questions A1 to A4 (the same as the workbook). Answers: A1) $120 (20 units: Monday 5 units, Tuesday 6 units; 11 units = $66, so 1 unit = $6) A2) 70 at first, 100 now (the blue beads did not change: 4 units at first, and 2 parts of 5 after, so 1 part = 2 units and the whole box is 10 units; red 3 units at first and 6 units now, so 3 units = 30 and 1 unit = 10) A3) 1 year ago (the difference, 32, is 4 units; 1 unit = 8: son 8, Mrs Tan 40) A4) $80 (Ben 2 units, Siti 1 unit + $20; 3 units = $120, 1 unit = $40)

p5l3-gofurther.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Go further questions B1 to B3 (the same as the workbook). Answers: B1) $60 (Siti spent 1 unit, Mei spent 3 units; the $120 difference is 2 units, so 1 unit = $60; both have $20 left) B2) 40 (work backwards: (4 + 4) × 2 = 16, (16 + 4) × 2 = 40) B3) 40 (Ali 3 units, keeps 2 units; Ben keeps 2 units, so Ben had 4 units; 7 units = 140, 1 unit = 20) Make up your own (printed under Go further): Make up a before-and-after story in which the total stays the same. Draw its model, then swap with a partner. Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks. Open-ended: check that a partner can solve it and that exactly one answer fits.

p5l3-gofurther2.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. These are the printed Go further questions B1 to B3 (the same as the workbook). Answers: B1) $60 (Siti spent 1 unit, Mei spent 3 units; the $120 difference is 2 units, so 1 unit = $60; both have $20 left) B2) 40 (work backwards: (4 + 4) × 2 = 16, (16 + 4) × 2 = 40) B3) 40 (Ali 3 units, keeps 2 units; Ben keeps 2 units, so Ben had 4 units; 7 units = 140, 1 unit = 20) Make up your own (printed under Go further): Make up a before-and-after story in which the total stays the same. Draw its model, then swap with a partner. Think for 30 seconds before anyone speaks. Open-ended: check that a partner can solve it and that exactly one answer fits.

p5l3-challenge.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. These are NOT on the workbook. Answers: 1) $48 (Ali has 3 units and keeps 2 after spending 1 unit; Ben has $90 − 3 units, and after spending $10 he has $80 − 3 units, which equals the 2 units Ali keeps; so 5 units = $80, 1 unit = $16; Ali $48, Ben $42; both have $32 left). 2) 6 years old (the difference is 3 units now and 1 unit in 12 years, so 3 old units = 1 new unit; Mei now 1 unit = 6, father 24; in 12 years 18 and 36).

p5l3-chdiag.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Show after pairs have tried Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the situation, not the answer. Ask: What stays the same in E1 after Ali and Ben spend? (They end up equal.) In E2, what stays the same? (The difference between the ages.) Which unit is "1 unit" in the later picture? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p5l3-chwalk.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some pairs are working or have finished, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Use after pairs have tried. E1: both start from different places but end equal, so the SPENT amounts matter: Ali spends 1 unit, Ben spends $10; Ali keeps 2 units and Ben keeps 2 units, so after spending the two have 4 units; the total after is 90 − 1 unit − 10. Check: Ali 48 spends 16 and keeps 32; Ben 42 spends 10 and keeps 32; 48 + 42 = 90 ✓. E2: the difference stays 3 units; in 12 years Mei is half, so the difference equals Mei's age then. Check: now 6 and 24 (6 is 1/4 of 24); later 18 and 36 (18 is half of 36) ✓.

p5l3-gap-r1.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it while some pairs are working or have finished, or use it live as an extra warm-up or tutor-bank question; never at a fixed minute, and it never takes time from the plan. ADDED ITEM r1 (a slide-only addition for the skill gap "What is a ratio?"; it is not in the printed workbook). TOOL: Draw it. PREVIEW LABEL: say "This is a first taste of a topic from a later level. We are not testing it; we are noticing how it works." SAY: A ratio compares two amounts with "for every". 2 : 3 means 2 blue for every 3 white. Draw the bars first, and call each box a unit. ASK: If Ali doubles the mix, what happens to both numbers? How many units are there in all in (b), and how big is one unit? LISTEN FOR: 2 : 3 = 4 : 6 (multiply both numbers by the same number). For (b): 2 + 3 = 5 units, 20 / 5 = 4 per unit, 2 x 4 = 8 and 3 x 4 = 12. Listen for "units" and "the same size". Do not teach more than this on the first meeting. Everyone writes the answer on their own paper, then say the answer together on three, then click the answer box. Nobody holds anything up, nobody is marked, and passing is always fine. ANSWER: (a) 6 tins of white, because 4 : 6 is the same ratio as 2 : 3. (b) 5 units altogether. One unit is 20 / 5 = 4 tins. Blue 8 tins, white 12 tins. WHY: Worked example for the tutor. Step 1: read the ratio as "for every": 2 blue for every 3 white. Step 2: draw 2 boxes and 3 boxes, equal size. Step 3: total units = 2 + 3 = 5. Step 4: one unit = 20 / 5 = 4. Step 5: blue = 2 x 4 = 8, white = 3 x 4 = 12. Step 6: check 8 + 12 = 20 and 8 : 12 = 2 : 3.

p5l3-gap-r2.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it while some pairs are working or have finished, or use it live as an extra warm-up or tutor-bank question; never at a fixed minute, and it never takes time from the plan. ADDED ITEM r2 (a slide-only addition for the skill gap "Equal ratios and simplest form"; it is not in the printed workbook). TOOL: Make a table. PREVIEW LABEL: say "This is a first taste of a topic from a later level. We are not testing it; we are noticing how it works." SAY: Make a table. Juice in the top row, water in the bottom row. Divide both numbers by 3 to get the smallest whole numbers, then multiply up. ASK: What do you do to both numbers to keep the ratio the same? How do you know 2 : 3 is simplest and cannot go smaller? LISTEN FOR: The same number on both sides (multiply or divide). Simplest form means no whole number other than 1 divides both. 10 cups of juice is 5 groups of 2, so 5 x 3 = 15. Everyone writes the answer on their own paper, then say the answer together on three, then click the answer box. Nobody holds anything up, nobody is marked, and passing is always fine. ANSWER: (a) 6 : 9. (b) 2 : 3 (divide both numbers by 3). (c) 15 cups of water. (d) 18. WHY: 6 : 9 divided by 3 gives 2 : 3. For 10 cups of juice: 10 = 5 x 2, so water is 5 x 3 = 15. For (d): 12 = 6 x 2, so the box is 6 x 3 = 18. SAME SKILL, NEW NUMBERS (tutor bank, say it aloud or write it on the board): A paint mix is 8 tins of red for every 12 tins of yellow. Write the ratio in simplest form. How many tins of yellow go with 14 tins of red? Answer: 2 : 3; 21 tins.

p5l3-gap-r3.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it while some pairs are working or have finished, or use it live as an extra warm-up or tutor-bank question; never at a fixed minute, and it never takes time from the plan. ADDED ITEM r3 (a slide-only addition for the skill gap "Sharing in a ratio"; it is not in the printed workbook). TOOL: Draw it. PREVIEW LABEL: say "This is a first taste of a topic from a later level. We are not testing it; we are noticing how it works." SAY: Draw a bar for Mei with 4 boxes and a bar for Siti with 5 boxes, the same size. The 45 stickers fill all the boxes. ASK: How can you check your answer? What do you notice about the difference between the two shares and one part? LISTEN FOR: 4 + 5 = 9 parts, 45 / 9 = 5. Mei 4 x 5 = 20, Siti 5 x 5 = 25, total 45. The difference 5 is 1 part because 5 - 4 = 1. Listen for the check: the two shares add up to 45. Everyone writes the answer on their own paper, then say the answer together on three, then click the answer box. Nobody holds anything up, nobody is marked, and passing is always fine. ANSWER: (a) 9 parts. (b) 5 stickers. (c) Mei 20 stickers and Siti 25 stickers. (d) 5 more stickers. WHY: One part is 45 / 9 = 5 stickers. Mei: 4 x 5 = 20. Siti: 5 x 5 = 25. The shares add to 45, and their ratio 20 : 25 is 4 : 5 when both are divided by 5. SAME SKILL, NEW NUMBERS (tutor bank, say it aloud or write it on the board): Ravi and Aisha share 56 marbles in the ratio 3 : 5. How many marbles does each get? Answer: Ravi 21 marbles, Aisha 35 marbles.

p5l3-talk.note: Minutes 71.5 to 77. Pairs talk for 2 minutes, then share. Answer: Yes. If Ali gives Mei 20 marbles, Ali has 30 and Mei has 50: the difference is 20 again, but now Mei has more. The total is 80 the whole time. Ask: "When does the total stay the same? When does the difference stay the same?" (Giving between two people keeps the total. Both getting or spending the same keeps the difference.) Praise the reasons, not only the answers. Protected think time: before anyone speaks, everyone thinks silently for 30 seconds (show the clock). Then pairs talk. This applies to the explore, to the talk question and to any make-up-your-own prompt. The Investigation first step is take-home (or the opener of the next lesson): tell the group so at the end of the talk time. Talk-time rules: say "You may say pass." Ask for VOLUNTEERS first, then invite others only if they want to. No cold-calling by name, no public tallies or rankings, and no "who got it right?" hands. Talk time: 30 seconds of silent thinking, 2 minutes pairs talk, 1 and a half minutes volunteers share, then tell everyone that the first step of the Investigation (the page after workbook page 2) is take-home, or the opener of the next lesson. Pass is always allowed.

p5l3-exit.note: Minutes 77 to 83. Answer: 15 (the total stays 60; 3 units = 60, so Ali has 1 unit = 20 at the end: 35 − 20 = 15) Extension: Make up your own before-and-after story where the total stays the same and the answer is 24. Swap with a partner and solve each other’s story with a model.

p5l3-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 83 to 85.5. Start the timer (90 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals. After the look-back, minutes 85.5 to 90 are flex time (the buffer): finish stamps, then goodbye. Do not start anything new.
